docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Agential control represents the capacity to initiate and modify actions based on ongoing assessment rather than responding automatically to environmental triggers.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text: Ferdman draws on skill philosophy to establish that: - Skills require control over initiating the task - Habits are merely elicited in response to environmental triggers - The development of agential control involves a shift in the balance between automaticity and control through a process of tuning and attuning

docs.title: Critical Distinction: Plan-Forming vs Plan-Following
docs.text:
The paper introduces a crucial framework for understanding agential control in AI contexts:

Dimension Plan-Forming Plan-Following Agency Full agential control Habitual response Initiation Self-directed Triggered by environment Responsibility Personal accountability External attribution Capacity Development Builds cognitive musculature Atrophies judgment

As Ferdman states: "To cultivate a skill is to develop flexible links between thought and action, such that continue to evolve even after expertise has been achieved."

docs.title: Impact on Market Research Roles
docs.text: AI systems that encourage plan-following rather than plan-forming create significant risks for professional development: - Entry-level researchers who only execute pre-determined analysis protocols fail to develop the agential control needed for complex problem-solving - AI-powered research tools that automatically generate insights eliminate opportunities to practice forming research questions and interpretation frameworks - Automated reporting systems that produce finished deliverables deprive analysts of the habituation process necessary for developing judgment

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Ferdman cites evidence that "indiscriminately automating human activity may create capacity-hostile environments, insofar as users will be deprived of the habituation process necessary for properly developing the capacities involved in routine activities." This explains why high-intensity AI adopters who maintain opportunities for agential control see 12.0% growth in entry-level roles, while those creating plan-following environments experience the entry-level-squeeze.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text: Organizations can foster agential control by: 1. Designing AI tools that require human initiation of key processes 2. Creating "red team" opportunities where staff must challenge AI-generated insights 3. Implementing structured reflection sessions after project completion 4. Ensuring junior staff have opportunities to formulate research questions before analysis begins

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept is central to understanding the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies problem and represents a key ai-adoption-methodological-innovation addressed by the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study. It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: AI Deskilling is a Structural Problem
docs.text: The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Unlike traditional deskilling (which refers to the obsolescence of specific job skills), AI deskilling targets core human capacities that are constitutive of human flourishing.

docs.title: Capacity vs. Skill
docs.text:
• Skills: Domain-specific expertise (hunting, coding, writing) that can become obsolete through technological change
  • Capacities: Core human abilities (epistemic, social, creative, volitional) that constitute human flourishing

While skill obsolescence has always been part of human history, capacity-deskilling is problematic because inadequate development of these core capacities diminishes us as humans.

docs.title: Mechanisms of AI Deskilling
docs.text:
1. Automation of Routine Tasks: Deprives users of opportunities to "practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025), leaving them unprepared for exceptional circumstances.

  2. Narrow Fields of Affordances: Creates environments with limited action possibilities that restrict opportunities for capacity development and exercise.

  3. Reduced Embodied Interaction: Limits physical presence and sensory experience necessary for developing social and moral capacities.

  4. Diminished Intersubjectivity: Reduces opportunities for shared valuing of capacities through human relationships and mentorship.

  5. Plan-Following Environments: Encourages users to respond to AI-generated recommendations rather than exercising agential control through self-deliberation (see plan-forming-vs-plan-following).

docs.title: Evidence of Deskilling
docs.text: Research shows growing evidence of: - Erosion of critical thinking and decision-making (Bonicalzi et al. 2023; Lee et al. 2025) - Decline in analytical reasoning (Zhai et al. 2024) - In healthcare: diminished diagnostic reasoning, declining clinical judgment, reduced retention of tacit knowledge, declining ethical sensitivity, and weakened moral judgment (NHS England 2023; Natali et al. 2025; Budzyń et al. 2025) - Young people struggling with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, and problem-solving (Halliday 2025)

docs.title: Structural Perspective
docs.text: The key insight from ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem is that deskilling should not be framed as an individual responsibility problem. Rather than expecting people to "will themselves to cultivate 'the arts of personhood,'" we should ask "what kind of socio-technical environments would be best for the cultivation of our personhood."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In the market research industry, AI deskilling manifests as: - The entry-level-squeeze phenomenon, where AI automates foundational research tasks that historically served as training grounds - Reduced opportunities for researchers to develop judgment through hands-on experience - Diminished capacity for creative insight generation when AI tools provide immediate answers - Erosion of ethical sensitivity when AI systems make moral decisions without transparent reasoning

Market research organizations should evaluate AI tools not just on efficiency metrics but on how they support or undermine researchers' capacity to engage meaningfully with data, clients, and research subjects.

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

AI professionalization refers to the process where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans. This phenomenon represents one pathway through which AI reshapes occupations, increasing the premium on specialized human expertise.

docs.title: New Evidence and Refinement
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study provides compelling evidence of AI professionalization in the insights industry: - As AI handles routine analytical tasks, value is shifting upstream toward strategic functions - Insights teams must evolve from delivering answers to shaping decisions, driving growth, and influencing strategy - Pam Forbus of [[mondelez]] states: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

This represents a specific manifestation of professionalization where AI automation of basic tasks elevates the importance of strategic human capabilities.

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development
docs.text:
A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.title: Connection to Entry-Level Dynamics
docs.text: The burning-glass-beyond-binary report shows that professionalization occurs alongside automation within the same occupations. This creates particular challenges for entry-level positions through the entry-level-squeeze, as foundational tasks that build expertise are automated before new developmental pathways are established.

docs.title: Organizational Implications
docs.text: Successful navigation of AI professionalization requires: - Redesigning roles to preserve meaningful human involvement in value-creating activities - Developing new apprenticeship models that build expertise despite automated foundational tasks - Aligning skill development priorities with the evolving value chain

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, providing alternatives to capacity-hostile-environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
• Rich affordance space: Provides diverse action possibilities that trigger multiple human capacities simultaneously
  • Embodied interaction: Supports physical presence and sensory experience essential for social and moral skill development
  • Intersubjective learning: Facilitates transmission of both technical knowledge and shared valuing of capacities
  • Agential control opportunities: Creates contexts where individuals must initiate and adjust actions rather than respond to environmental triggers

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
1. Hybrid research methodologies that combine AI-powered data collection with human-led interpretation sessions
  2. Mentorship programs where junior researchers observe and participate in client consultations alongside experienced professionals
  3. Collaborative analysis workshops where teams collectively interpret findings, developing shared understanding through embodied discussion
  4. Ethnographic fieldwork that requires physical presence and sensory engagement with research subjects

docs.title: Implementation Framework
docs.text:
Based on Ferdman's analysis, capacity-conducive environments should include:

Component Implementation in Market Research Embodied engagement Regular in-person team sessions, fieldwork opportunities, client meetings Intersubjective valuing Structured reflection sessions, shared project debriefs, storytelling about professional growth Gradual habituation Scaffolded learning pathways from observation to independent practice Agential control Opportunities for junior staff to initiate research questions and methodology choices

docs.title: Contrast with capacity-hostile-environments
docs.text:
While capacity-hostile environments create a vicious cycle of capacity impoverishment, capacity-conducive environments foster a virtuous cycle: 1. Rich opportunities for engagement → 2. Deep development of capacities → 3. Appreciation of mastery in those capacities → 4. Further investment in capacity cultivation

This framework explains why high-intensity AI adopters like [[high-intensity-ai-adopters]] can grow entry-level roles by 12.0% - they've created capacity-conducive environments where AI augments rather than replaces human development.

docs.title: Research Evidence
docs.text: Ferdman demonstrates that capacity-conducive environments must go beyond merely affording opportunities for capacity exercise - they must actively encourage such engagement. This requires public goods like community spaces, quality public areas, and structured professional development opportunities that foster embodied interaction.

docs.title: Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: Environments that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These environments undermine the process of capacity cultivation by providing inadequate conditions for developing and exercising human capacities.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
1. Narrow Field of Affordances: Provide limited action possibilities that restrict opportunities for engaging in activities requiring competent exercise of capacities.

  2. Shallow Skilling Opportunities: Afford opportunities for shallow development of capacities but restrict opportunities for fuller, well-rounded development.

  3. Discouraged Embodiment: Limit physical presence and sensory experience necessary for developing social and moral capacities.

  4. Reduced Intersubjectivity: Limit opportunities for shared valuing of capacities through human relationships and mentorship.

  5. Plan-Following Orientation: Encourage responding to environmental triggers rather than exercising agential control through self-initiated activities.

docs.title: Examples in AI Context
docs.text:
1. Healthcare AI Systems: Afford offloading tasks to machines, leading to automation bias where users attribute excessive trust to AI tools. This risks loss of critical skills necessary for unexpected scenarios like system malfunctions (Natali et al. 2025).

  2. Smartphones: Provide disconnected interaction possibilities (swiping, clicking, scrolling) that fracture users' affordance space into disconnected fields, leading to alienation rather than offering opportunities for mutually informing cognitive and bodily skills (Butler 2024).

  3. Artificial Personal Assistants: Constantly available AI tools that replace human activity in life-planning and decision-making, discouraging users from seeking alternative avenues to exercise their capacities (see artificial-personal-assistants).

docs.title: Structural Harm
docs.text: Capacity-hostile environments are normatively problematic when they lead to "affordance shrinkage" that is: - Systematic - Enduring - Deeply entrenched - Discouraging users from finding ways to compensate for the shrinkage

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Unlike capacity-conducive environments, which actively encourage capacity development through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, capacity-hostile environments undermine the structural conditions necessary for human flourishing.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text: In market research, capacity-hostile environments might include: - AI tools that automate the entire research process without opportunities for researchers to exercise judgment - Research platforms that limit embodied interaction with research participants - Analytics systems that provide immediate answers without requiring researchers to engage in the habituation process of developing analytical skills - Environments that encourage plan-following (executing pre-determined research protocols) rather than plan-forming (creatively designing research approaches)

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text: Creative capacities are the human abilities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces. These capacities constitute a fundamental component of human flourishing, as they enable individuals to innovate, express themselves, and adapt to novel situations. According to Developmental Perfectionism (see developmental-perfectionism), the competent exercise of creative capacities yields intrinsically valuable outcomes like artistic expression, innovative solutions, and conceptual breakthroughs.

docs.title: Characteristics of Creative Capacities
docs.text:
1. Novel Combination: The ability to make unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas, going beyond mere association to create something genuinely new.

  2. Conceptual Transformation: The capacity to transform a conceptual space, altering how we understand and navigate domains of thought or practice.

  3. Non-Mechanical Process: Creativity involves more than luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures; it requires intentional engagement with the creative process.

  4. Value Judgment: Creative work involves discerning which novel combinations have value and merit further development.

docs.title: Development of Creative Capacities
docs.text:
Creative capacities develop through a gradual process of habituation (see habituation-process), characterized by:

  • Embodied Exploration: Physical engagement with materials, environments, and sensory experiences is essential for developing creative capacities (see embodiment-in-skilling).

  • Intersubjective Feedback: Creative development depends on relationships with mentors and peers who provide constructive criticism and share the value of creative work (see intersubjectivity-in-skilling).

  • Agential Control: The ability to adjust the creative process as it unfolds, distinguishing skilled creation from habitual or automated production (see agential-control).

  • Plan-Forming: Creativity often involves actively creating new pathways through self-deliberation rather than merely following pre-determined creative templates (see plan-forming-vs-plan-following).

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, AI systems can undermine creative capacities through:

  1. Premature Closure: AI tools that provide immediate creative outputs may discourage the exploratory process necessary for genuine creativity.

  2. Reduced Practice: Automating creative tasks deprives users of opportunities to develop their own creative muscles through trial and error.

  3. Homogenization: AI systems trained on existing data may reinforce conventional patterns rather than encouraging truly novel combinations.

  4. Erosion of Creative Judgment: Over-reliance on AI for creative decisions can diminish the ability to discern valuable creative work.

docs.title: Evidence of Erosion
docs.text: Research cited in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem shows growing evidence of: - Erosion of critical thinking and decision-making as a result of over-reliance on artificial intelligence - In healthcare, AI dependence has been found to diminish diagnostic reasoning and clinical judgment - Young people growing up with smartphones struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like problem-solving

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In market research, creative capacities are essential for: - Designing innovative research methodologies - Interpreting ambiguous data in novel ways - Developing compelling insights and storytelling - Creating engaging research experiences for participants - Adapting research approaches to novel market situations

AI tools that automate insight generation or research design without preserving opportunities for researchers to exercise these capacities risk creating capacity-hostile environments that ultimately degrade the innovative potential of market research.

docs.title: Developmental Perfectionism
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism is a neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life (Hurka 1993). According to this framework, humans exercise their capacities in activities that yield outcomes with intrinsic value like knowledge, beauty, morality, and friendship (Kraut 2013; Bradford 2016, 2021; Fletcher 2016). The competent exercise of human capacities is the manifestation of achieving intrinsically valuable goods, making the capacities themselves intrinsically valuable.

This philosophical framework is critical for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. As Avigail Ferdman argues in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, capacity-deskilling is bad because human capacities are constitutive of our flourishing. Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives. For example, the value of being on the summit of a mountain is gained from the competent exercise of climbing capacities, not from simply being there (say, if one arrives there by helicopter).

Developmental Perfectionism provides the normative foundation for evaluating AI applications based on their conduciveness or hostility to capacity cultivation. It shifts the focus from individual responsibility for cultivating capacities to the societal obligation to foster environments that support human flourishing.

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text:
1. Intrinsically Valuable Goods: Activities that yield knowledge, beauty, morality, and friendship have intrinsic value.

  2. Competent Exercise: The value comes from competently exercising capacities, not merely achieving outcomes.

  3. Unified Life: Flourishing involves a complex, well-rounded integration of multiple capacities rather than excelling in isolated domains.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text: In the market research industry, Developmental Perfectionism suggests that AI tools should be evaluated not just on efficiency metrics but on how they support or undermine researchers' capacity to engage meaningfully with data, clients, and research subjects. Tools that automate the entire research process without opportunities for researchers to exercise judgment risk creating capacity-hostile environments.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Embodiment represents the physical foundation of capacity cultivation, emphasizing that many human capacities cannot be fully developed through disembodied interaction.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman draws on enactive cognition approaches to demonstrate that:

  • Embodied 'participatory sense-making' is constitutive of social cognition
  • Moral attention requires perceiving others as embodied beings through voice and gaze
  • Social interaction dynamics constitute an essential part of the cognitive process
  • The spontaneity of recognizing others as moral agents is inherent in embodied interaction

*'Without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents. The spontaneity of recognizing the other as moral agent is inherent in the embodied interaction...'

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
Embodiment is particularly critical in market research due to the field's reliance on:

  • Nonverbal communication: Reading body language and emotional cues in qualitative research
  • Contextual understanding: Developing nuanced insights through physical presence in research environments
  • Trust building: Establishing client relationships through face-to-face interaction
  • Ethical judgment: Making morally complex decisions that require embodied moral sensitivity

docs.title: AI Threats to Embodiment
docs.text:
AI systems undermine embodied skilling through:

  1. Disembodied interfaces: Replacing face-to-face client and participant interactions with digital platforms

  2. Automated analysis: Reducing opportunities for researchers to develop embodied pattern recognition through direct data engagement

  3. Virtual collaboration: Encouraging remote work patterns that minimize physical team interaction

  4. Reduced fieldwork: AI-powered remote research methods decreasing opportunities for embodied research experiences

As Ferdman notes regarding friendship development:

'Disembodied interactions make it harder to form meaningful friendship because technologically mediated virtue friendships require more discipline for a diminished experience.'

This applies equally to professional relationships in market research, where embodied interaction is essential for developing the trust and shared understanding necessary for high-quality insights.

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To maintain embodiment in AI-augmented research:

  • Preserve opportunities for face-to-face client workshops and presentations
  • Design hybrid research methods that combine AI efficiency with embodied fieldwork
  • Create physical collaboration spaces that encourage team interaction
  • Implement 'embodiment audits' to assess critical research activities requiring physical presence
  • Develop training programs that emphasize embodied research skills

docs.title: Measurement Framework
docs.text:
Organizations can assess embodiment in skilling through: - Ratio of face-to-face to digital client interactions - Opportunities for embodied field research experiences - Quality of physical collaboration spaces - Frequency of embodied team reflection sessions

See also: intersubjectivity-in-skilling, capacity-conducive-environments, human-capacities

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text: Epistemic capacities are the human abilities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding. These capacities constitute a fundamental component of human flourishing, as they enable individuals to navigate truth, form justified beliefs, and make informed decisions. According to Developmental Perfectionism (see developmental-perfectionism), the competent exercise of epistemic capacities yields intrinsically valuable outcomes.

docs.title: Components of Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
1. Theoretical Rationality: The capacity for thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, and contemplating. This involves:
  2. Critical evaluation of evidence
  3. Logical reasoning
  4. Conceptual analysis
  5. Intellectual curiosity

  6. Openness to revising beliefs

  7. Practical Rationality (Phronesis): Often translated as "practical wisdom" or "common sense," this capacity enables individuals to:

  8. Determine effective means to ends
  9. Accurately assess situations and circumstances
  10. Exercise discernment in applying general principles to specific contexts
  11. Make sound judgments in complex, ambiguous situations
  12. Coordinate multiple goals and intentions

docs.title: Development of Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
Epistemic capacities develop through a gradual process of habituation (see habituation-process), characterized by:

  • Embodied Learning: Physical presence and sensory experience are essential for developing epistemic capacities, particularly in social contexts (see embodiment-in-skilling).

  • Intersubjective Guidance: Learning from mentors and peers who model good reasoning practices and share the value of epistemic virtues (see intersubjectivity-in-skilling).

  • Agential Control: The ability to adjust one's reasoning process as it unfolds, distinguishing skilled reasoning from habitual or automated responses (see agential-control).

  • Plan-Forming: Actively creating reasoning pathways through self-deliberation rather than merely following pre-determined reasoning templates (see plan-forming-vs-plan-following).

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, AI systems can undermine epistemic capacities through:

  1. Automation Bias: Over-reliance on AI outputs can diminish critical evaluation skills and diagnostic reasoning.

  2. Reduced Practice: Automating routine analytical tasks deprives users of opportunities to "practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature."

  3. Shallow Engagement: AI tools that provide immediate answers may discourage deep, sustained engagement with complex problems.

  4. Erosion of Epistemic Autonomy: When AI systems make decisions without transparent reasoning, users may lose the ability to independently assess claims.

docs.title: Evidence of Erosion
docs.text: Research cited in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem shows growing evidence of: - Erosion of critical thinking (Bonicalzi et al. 2023; Lee et al. 2025) - Decline in decision-making and analytical reasoning (Zhai et al. 2024) - Diminished diagnostic reasoning in healthcare professionals - Reduced retention of tacit knowledge

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In market research, epistemic capacities are essential for: - Interpreting ambiguous consumer data - Designing valid research methodologies - Drawing meaningful insights from complex information - Communicating findings with appropriate nuance

AI tools that automate data analysis without preserving opportunities for researchers to exercise these capacities risk creating capacity-hostile environments that ultimately degrade research quality and insight generation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Core Characteristics
docs.text:
• Gradual progression: Moves through stages from novice to expert (Dreyfus & Dreyfus 5-stage model)
  • Experience-based: Requires concrete experience rather than abstract principles
  • Error-driven refinement: Involves learning from mistakes and overcoming disappointment
  • Time-intensive: Demands considerable time and living to develop mastery

docs.title: 1. Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
• Requires mentors to guide novices into proper motivational structures
  • Involves transmission of both technical knowledge and shared valuing of the skill
  • Creates "shared intentions" and "shared valuing" between mentor and mentee
  • Social practices at scale (family, colleagues, citizens) provide mentoring environments

docs.title: 2. Embodiment
docs.text:
• Depends on physical presence and sensory experience
  • Requires "embodied understanding" through voice, gaze, and shared physical space
  • Enables "participatory sense-making" in social cognition
  • Creates shared history and embodied interaction essential for skill development

docs.title: AI's Disruptive Impact
docs.text:
Ferdman demonstrates how AI systems threaten the habituation process through:

Threat Mechanism Consequence Automation bias Offloading tasks to AI systems Deprives users of routine opportunities to strengthen "cognitive musculature" Disembodied interaction Digital mediation replacing physical presence Undermines embodied understanding critical to social capacities Shallow engagement Fragmented digital experiences Prevents deep attunement to individual cases Reduced error exposure AI providing "correct" answers Eliminates learning from mistakes and disappointment

docs.title: Evidence from Market Research
docs.text: The paper cites evidence that "automating routine tasks and leaving only exception-handling to the human user, 'deprives the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature, leaving them atrophied and unprepared when the exceptions do arise.'" This explains the growing entry-level-squeeze phenomenon where entry-level positions increasingly lack the habituation opportunities necessary for professional development.

docs.title: Creating Habituation-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Organizations can protect the habituation process by: - Designing AI tools that preserve opportunities for embodied interaction - Ensuring junior staff have structured opportunities for guided practice - Creating safe spaces for making and learning from mistakes - Maintaining human-led mentoring relationships alongside AI tools - Preserving opportunities for shared valuing of professional capacities

docs.title: Human Capacities
docs.text: Human capacities are the core abilities that constitute human flourishing, as identified in philosophical literature on human nature and well-being. According to Developmental Perfectionism (see developmental-perfectionism), these capacities are not merely instrumental but are constitutive of a flourishing human life. When humans competently develop and exercise these capacities, they lead flourishing lives.

docs.title: Core Human Capacities
docs.text:
1. Epistemic Capacities: Include theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating) and practical rationality (manifesting in phronesis or practical wisdom). These capacities enable humans to navigate truth, knowledge, and reasoning in both abstract and concrete contexts.

  2. Social Capacities: Encompass moral capacity as well as social and caring capacities for developing meaningful relationships of friendship and love. These capacities allow humans to form connections, understand others' perspectives, and participate in communal life.

  3. Creative Capacities: Involve making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas, transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures. Creativity enables humans to innovate, express themselves, and adapt to novel situations.

  4. Volitional Capacity: The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow to achieve intrinsically valuable goals. This capacity is treated as a meta-capacity because developing and exercising any of the other human capacities requires willpower.

docs.title: Characteristics of Human Capacities
docs.text:
• Interdependence: Human capacities rarely operate in isolation (Kraut 2007). For example, the capacity to know involves theoretical rationality, practical rationality, volitional capacity, and physical capacities.

  • Gradual Development: Capacities develop through a slow process of habituation (see habituation-process), requiring practice, feedback, and time.

  • Embodied Nature: Capacities are developed and exercised through physical presence and sensory experience (see embodiment-in-skilling).

  • Intersubjective Dimension: Capacity development depends on relationships with others who guide and share the value of the capacity (see intersubjectivity-in-skilling).

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, AI systems can undermine human capacities through:

  1. Automation of Routine Tasks: Depriving users of opportunities to "practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025).

  2. Narrow Fields of Affordances: Creating environments with limited action possibilities that restrict capacity development.

  3. Reduced Embodied Interaction: Limiting opportunities for physical presence and sensory experience necessary for capacity cultivation.

  4. Diminished Intersubjectivity: Reducing opportunities for shared valuing of capacities through human relationships.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In market research, human capacities are essential for: - Interpreting nuanced consumer behavior - Building rapport with research participants - Creatively designing research methodologies - Exercising judgment when data is ambiguous

AI tools that automate these processes without preserving opportunities for researchers to exercise these capacities risk creating capacity-hostile environments that ultimately degrade research quality.

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Intersubjectivity represents the social foundation of capacity cultivation, emphasizing that skill development is inherently relational rather than purely individual.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman draws on social philosophy to demonstrate that:

  • Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to guide the novice into becoming an expert
  • Mentors instill not only mechanical aspects of the skill but, as importantly, the value of the skill
  • In the mentor-mentee relationship, both parties develop 'shared valuing' of the skill
  • Social practices performed by groups or whole societies provide mentoring environments

'In the relationship between mentor and novice, the mentor instills not only the mechanical aspects of the skill, but, as importantly, the value of the skill, such that in the process of habituation, the skilled agent eventually comes to view the value of the skill as their own.'

docs.title: Market Research Context
docs.text:
Intersubjectivity in skilling is particularly critical in market research due to the field's reliance on:

  • Shared understanding of client needs: Developing the capacity to interpret ambiguous client requests
  • Collective insight generation: Building shared frameworks for interpreting complex data
  • Ethical judgment: Cultivating shared values around research ethics and participant treatment
  • Creative problem-solving: Developing shared approaches to novel research challenges

docs.title: AI Threats to Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
AI systems undermine intersubjective skilling through:

  1. Reduced mentorship opportunities: Automated tools handle routine tasks that previously provided mentorship contexts

  2. Disembodied interaction: Digital mediation reduces opportunities for the 'shared history and participatory sense-making' essential to skill development

  3. Individualized AI assistance: Personal AI tools create isolated learning experiences rather than shared ones

  4. Value misalignment: AI systems may instill efficiency values over deeper research excellence values

As Ferdman warns:

'When enough persons do not value excellence or mastery of a human capacity (e.g., critical thinking), the capacity is in danger of atrophying. First, the agent would not have the proper mentoring of the 'know-how', and second, they would not obtain the shared understanding regarding the value of the capacities.'

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To maintain intersubjectivity in AI-augmented research:

  • Design AI tools that facilitate rather than replace mentorship conversations
  • Create structured team review processes for AI-generated outputs
  • Implement 'shared reflection sessions' after AI-assisted projects
  • Preserve opportunities for embodied team collaboration
  • Develop organizational frameworks for shared valuing of research excellence

docs.title: Measurement Framework
docs.text:
Organizations can assess intersubjective skilling through: - Frequency of structured mentorship interactions - Quality of shared reflection on research processes - Alignment between individual and organizational research values - Opportunities for embodied team collaboration

See also: embodiment-in-skilling, habituation-process, capacity-conducive-environments

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Affordances represent the action possibilities formed by the relationship between an agent and its environment.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman builds on Gibson's ecological psychology to explain that:

  • Affordances are not mere opportunities but invitations that influence agent behavior
  • The environment is a 'world of affordances' that is constitutive of flourishing
  • Proper cultivation of core capacities depends on inhabiting environments that afford action possibilities for relevant activities

'The concept of affordances helps explain how the environment is constitutive of flourishing: the proper cultivation of the core capacities is dependent on inhabiting an environment that affords action possibilities for activities, in turn triggering the capacities associated with these activities.'

docs.title: AI-Induced Narrowing
docs.text:
AI systems narrow the field of affordances through:

  1. Automation bias: Creating environments where offloading tasks to AI becomes the default option

  2. Reduced exception handling: Automating routine tasks while leaving only exception-handling to humans, 'depriving the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature'

  3. Deterministic interfaces: Designing systems that invite 'determinate, separate, and repeatable tasks' rather than complex, integrated activities

  4. Feedback reduction: Limiting opportunities for learning from mistakes through AI's error-reduction capabilities

docs.title: Market Research Examples
docs.text:
1. Automated insight generation platforms that provide ready-made interpretations, narrowing affordances for researcher interpretation and critical analysis

  2. AI-powered research design tools that generate standardized methodologies, reducing opportunities for creative research design

  3. Chatbot client interfaces that handle routine inquiries, narrowing affordances for junior researchers to develop relationship management skills

  4. Predictive analytics systems that present single forecast scenarios rather than multiple possibilities, reducing opportunities for strategic thinking

docs.title: Affordance Shrinkage
docs.text:
Ferdman distinguishes between temporary affordance reduction and problematic 'affordance shrinkage'—when the reduction in action possibilities is systematic, enduring, and deeply entrenched such that it discourages users from finding ways to compensate.

In market research, affordance shrinkage occurs when: - AI tools become the only approved methodology for certain research activities - Organizational culture discourages 'non-standard' research approaches - Performance metrics prioritize AI efficiency over capacity development - Training programs focus exclusively on AI tool usage rather than foundational research skills

docs.title: Expanding Affordances
docs.text:
To counter narrow fields of affordances, organizations should:

  • Design AI tools with multiple pathways rather than single solutions
  • Implement 'capacity cultivation zones' where AI assistance is deliberately limited
  • Create structured opportunities for researchers to exercise agential control
  • Develop metrics that value capacity development alongside productivity

docs.title: Measurement Framework
docs.text:
Organizations can assess field of affordances through: - Diversity of action possibilities in AI-augmented workflows - Opportunities for researcher-initiated modifications - Balance between AI recommendations and researcher autonomy - Frequency of exception-handling scenarios that require human judgment

See also: capacity-hostile-environments, agential-control, habituation-process

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This distinction represents a fundamental mechanism through which AI systems can undermine human capacities.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman draws on Bratman's theory of agency to explain that:

  • Plan-forming involves two critical agential functions:
  • Settling function: Managing finite cognitive resources when facing choices

  • Coordination function: Forming and organizing different types of plans and intentions

  • Plan-following involves responding to triggers in the environment without initiating the planning process

'Forming a plan by self-deliberation requires exercising control over all the steps of the activity of forming the plan, including over initiating the two functions of planning: settling (deciding between options) and coordinating.'

docs.title: Capacity Implications
docs.text:
The plan-forming vs. plan-following distinction has profound implications for capacity development:

  • Plan-forming requires exercising epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities, as well as the capacity to will
  • Plan-following involves a shallower exercise of capacities, primarily responding to environmental triggers
  • Transition from plan-forming to plan-following represents a shift from skilled activity to habitual response

As Ferdman explains:

'In plan-forming, the capacity to will is involved in initiating the plan, whereas in plan-following, it is absent, because the user is responding to a trigger in the environment—the APA output.'

docs.title: Market Research Examples
docs.text:
1. Research design:
  2. Plan-forming: Researcher develops methodology through self-deliberation on research questions, client needs, and resource constraints

  3. Plan-following: Researcher accepts AI-generated methodology without modification

  4. Insight interpretation:

  5. Plan-forming: Researcher develops interpretation framework through engagement with data and client context

  6. Plan-following: Researcher accepts AI-generated insights without critical evaluation

  7. Client recommendations:

  8. Plan-forming: Researcher develops strategic recommendations through consideration of multiple factors
  9. Plan-following: Researcher presents AI-generated recommendations without adaptation

docs.title: AI Threats to Plan-Forming
docs.text:
AI systems encourage plan-following through:

  • Constant availability: 'Always-on' interfaces that prompt users to seek assistance rather than initiate planning
  • Personalization: Tailoring advice to user preferences, reducing opportunities for challenging perspectives
  • Seamless integration: Making AI assistance the path of least resistance
  • Reduced cognitive load: Eliminating the effort required for self-deliberation

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To maintain plan-forming capacities in AI-augmented research:

  • Implement 'deliberation checkpoints' where researchers must formulate their own interpretations before viewing AI suggestions
  • Design AI tools that present multiple options rather than single recommendations
  • Create structured reflection processes after AI-assisted activities
  • Maintain human oversight for high-stakes research decisions
  • Develop training programs that emphasize practical wisdom development

docs.title: Measurement Framework
docs.text:
Organizations can assess plan-forming vs. plan-following through: - Ratio of researcher-initiated modifications to AI suggestions - Documentation of researcher deliberation processes - Opportunities for researcher input in AI-generated outputs - Frequency of critical evaluation of AI recommendations

See also: agential-control, [[practical-wisdom]], human-capacities

docs.title: Seniorised roles
docs.text: The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Seniorised roles describe the accelerating trend where entry-level positions now require skills traditionally associated with senior roles, driven by AI automation of foundational tasks. Figure 8 in the PwC 2026 report provides compelling evidence: in the US top AI exposure quartile, seniorised entry-level job postings are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This occurs because AI tools handle routine onboarding tasks (e.g., data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or basic analysis for [[recruiters]]), compressing career ladders and elevating entry requirements. Common senior skills now appearing in entry-level descriptions include strategic decision-making frameworks, cross-departmental collaboration, client advisory capabilities, and complex problem-solving—particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality if not balanced with structured mentorship, as new graduates face higher barriers without prior exposure to advanced skills. However, organizations using the ai-job-future-framework can mitigate risks by designing onboarding that combines AI tools with human skill development. The phenomenon represents a key manifestation of AI's impact on career progression, with implications for education systems needing to prepare students for accelerated responsibility in the AI era.

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text: Social capacities are the human abilities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life. These capacities constitute a fundamental component of human flourishing, as they enable individuals to connect with others, build trust, and contribute to shared social goods. According to Developmental Perfectionism (see developmental-perfectionism), the competent exercise of social capacities yields intrinsically valuable outcomes like friendship, love, and moral community.

docs.title: Components of Social Capacities
docs.text:
1. Moral Capacity: The ability to:
  2. Recognize moral considerations in situations
  3. Make sound ethical judgments
  4. Act in accordance with moral principles
  5. Develop moral sensitivity to others' experiences

  6. Navigate complex ethical dilemmas

  7. Relational Capacity: The ability to:

  8. Form and maintain meaningful relationships
  9. Express care and empathy
  10. Communicate effectively across differences
  11. Resolve conflicts constructively

  12. Build trust through consistent action

  13. Communal Capacity: The ability to:

  14. Participate in shared practices and institutions
  15. Contribute to collective goods
  16. Understand one's role within larger social structures
  17. Balance individual and communal interests

docs.title: Development of Social Capacities
docs.text:
Social capacities develop through a gradual process of habituation (see habituation-process), characterized by:

  • Embodied Interaction: Physical presence and sensory experience are essential for developing social capacities, particularly the ability to recognize others as moral agents through their voice and gaze (see embodiment-in-skilling).

  • Intersubjective Learning: Social capacities develop through relationships with others who model good social practices and share the value of social virtues (see intersubjectivity-in-skilling).

  • Shared Valuing: Becoming socially skilled involves internalizing the value of social capacities through participation in communities that affirm these values.

  • Gradual Refinement: Social capacities develop through successive trials, learning from mistakes, and encountering disappointment in relationships.

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, AI systems can undermine social capacities through:

  1. Disembodied Interaction: Digital environments that lack physical presence make it harder to form meaningful relationships and recognize others as moral agents.

  2. Reduced Practice: Automating social tasks (like communication or relationship management) deprives users of opportunities to develop social skills.

  3. Narrow Fields of Affordances: Environments that provide limited action possibilities for social engagement restrict opportunities for social capacity development.

  4. Erosion of Moral Sensitivity: Over-reliance on AI for moral decision-making can diminish ethical sensitivity and moral judgment.

docs.title: Evidence of Erosion
docs.text: Research cited in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem shows: - In healthcare, AI dependence has been found to diminish diagnostic reasoning, declining clinical judgment, reduced retention of tacit knowledge, declining ethical sensitivity, and weakened moral judgment (NHS England 2023; Natali et al. 2025; Budzyń et al. 2025). - Young people growing up with smartphones struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to other people, problem-solving, and critical thinking (Halliday 2025).

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
In market research, social capacities are essential for: - Building rapport with research participants - Conducting effective interviews and focus groups - Understanding nuanced consumer motivations - Navigating ethical considerations in research design - Collaborating effectively with team members and clients

AI tools that automate participant interaction or ethical decision-making without preserving opportunities for researchers to exercise these capacities risk creating capacity-hostile environments that ultimately degrade research quality and ethical standards.
